summary: Hoplight remote access is off by default and managed from Settings. Tailscale supplies an encrypted private link gated by the studio owner's numeric account identity, while LAN requires a random connect code followed by host approval. Trusted loopback requests use Host, Origin and session-token checks. Every Studio instance owns a separate ephemeral private loopback listener, passes its actual address to its helper, and authenticates it with a per-boot secret refused by the trusted door. Failed private binding disables mesh while local Studio and LAN remain available. Failed primary startup releases its private listener, and shutdown prevents deferred automatic resume. Host-only controls remain unavailable to remote clients. The helper is found in the source tree, beside the executable or in the product-specific support cache. Downloads require an explicitly published SHA-256 pin, bounded HTTPS fetching and verified bytes before installation. Locally supplied helpers carry no invented release marker; readiness can refresh without enabling mesh, and redownload is shown only when offered. Downloading leaves mesh off until a separate explicit Enable action. The manager kills only its owned child and ignores stale output. Local access resolves installed OpenSSL from PATH or standard Git for Windows directories. Startup failures are visible in Settings and permit retry. An isolated HTTPS regression checks the IP SAN, fingerprint and unapproved-device gate. Source tests do not establish installed-binary or physical-device behavior.

sections.title: Containers and SSH forwarding
sections.summary: Container or headless use does not need a browser inside that environment. The hoplight ui startup receipt prints the local Studio URL, one copyable SSH command for the Studio port, and when the isolated Lua regex listener started a second forward for its random sandbox port. Run it on the browser machine, replace user@server, keep the tunnel open, browse localhost with the printed ui-port. Browsing the server or container IP is refused by the trusted Host gate. HTML may arrive before api/settings is refused, so the browser turns that 403 into localhost and SSH instructions with Studio, Settings Remote access deep link, and one-port recovery copy buttons; host-only API gates still decide whether controls may change anything. One-port is enough for ordinary Studio work; Lua and regex benches need both ports because ADR-009 uses a second ephemeral loopback origin. Tailscale and LAN serve the approved Studio surface only and do not make the sandbox listener a general remote endpoint. This does not broaden hostAllowed, expose a new listener, or weaken token and Origin checks.

sections.title: Two listeners, one trust boundary
sections.summary: The trusted loopback listener defaults to port 8321 and requires the existing Host, Origin and session-token checks. Each Studio instance also binds its own ephemeral private loopback listener for the Tailscale helper. The actual bound address is passed to that helper, and every proxied request must carry the instance-specific per-boot CSPRNG secret. The secret travels through the child environment rather than argv and is refused by the trusted door. Another instance secret cannot authenticate this listener. A failed private bind leaves mesh unavailable while local Studio and LAN remain usable. Failed main-listener startup releases its already-created private listener, and closing before saved settings resolve prevents a later automatic mesh restart. LAN retains port 8790 and reports occupied-port failure rather than attaching to another app.
topics: untrusted 127.0.0.1 on an instance-owned ephemeral port

sections.title: The Tailscale owner gate
sections.summary: The sidecar embeds Tailscale via tsnet and for every remote request calls WhoIs on the caller tailnet address, admitting only the studio owner's own account. Identity is compared by numeric user id who.UserProfile.ID equals Self.UserID via resolveOwnerID and newProxy; login-name strings are not used because tsnet can return an empty login for the owner node while the numeric id is populated. Fail closed everywhere: unresolved owner id zero denies everyone; unidentifiable caller with no WhoIs is denied; a caller whose node has no stable id is denied because a device that cannot be tracked or kicked will not be served. Identity headers forwarded upstream X-Tailscale-User and X-Tailscale-Node are taken from WhoIs never from client-supplied headers so a forged header cannot survive. These properties are unit-tested against a fake resolver in sidecar main_test.go.

sections.title: The LAN gate: connect code + per-device approval
sections.summary: Without tailnet identity, LAN gates on two stranger-proof checks in lan-host. Connect code the owner reads off screen is CSPRNG with rejection sampling, argon2id-hashed via Bun.password, and never sent to the connecting device. Wrong guesses throttle per IP with exponential backoff never a global lockout. Right code makes a pending session served nothing until host approval; pending is capped per IP and expires after 15 minutes so the code alone cannot flood approvals or leave stale entries. Listener binds 0.0.0.0:8790 with self-signed TLS in lan-server so code and traffic never cross clear; cert puts LAN IP and loopback in subjectAltName, regenerates if cache misses current IP, private key chmod 600 best effort with Windows ACLs; owner verifies shown sha256 fingerprint. Nested why the session cookie is not Secure: approved cookie is HttpOnly SameSite Lax Path slash without Secure because self-signed is not a secure context in some browsers that silently drop Secure cookies.

children.title: Why the session cookie is not `Secure`
children.summary: The approved-session cookie is HttpOnly SameSite Lax Path slash with no Secure attribute in lan-server. The listener is HTTPS-only, but a self-signed cert is not a secure context in some browsers, which then silently DROP a Secure cookie and leave the device stuck re-entering the code forever. SameSite Lax lets the cookie ride the reload navigation; HttpOnly still stands.

sections.title: Host-only surface
sections.summary: Whether a device tailed in over Tailscale or was approved on the LAN, it may USE the studio but must never reach management or host control. isHostOnlyRoute in server-remote refuses for any remote or LAN-served handler every api/remote route that turns access on or off or kicks devices, api/open that opens a browser on the host, api/shutdown, api/restart, and settings writes. Those belong to the local owner alone.

sections.title: Kicking a device
sections.summary: The owner can remove any connected device from the host. Over Tailscale the app writes a kick command to the sidecar stdin; the sidecar blocklists that node stable id and denies it on the next request even though it is the owner own account via deviceTracker in main.go. On LAN the session is dropped.

sections.title: Where the sidecar binary comes from
sections.summary: The sidecar is compiled Go and is not inside Hoplight.exe. sidecarCandidates in server-remote checks three locations in order: the repository sidecar folder that bun sidecar/build.ts writes, a sidecar folder beside the running executable, and the aux-package cache where a requested download installs it. None present reports unavailable, its own RemotePhase distinct from off and error, because off is a switch the owner can flip and error invites a retry while a build with no helper can do neither; the panel says so up front and offers no Enable control instead of spawning a path that is not there. LAN mode needs no helper. The beside-the-executable candidate is load-bearing: deriving the path from import.meta.url alone is correct from source and meaningless once compiled, resolving onto the Bun virtual filesystem, so every packaged studio failed to start remote access and surfaced a raw uv_spawn ENOENT. Pinned by server-remote.test.ts.

sections.title: The aux package: fetching the helper on request
sections.summary: The helper is a separate release asset fetched only by an explicit host action. Committed SHA-256 pins are reviewed like dependencies; the pinning script downloads every selected asset and verifies it against the release checksum inventory. The protocol is version-compatible independently of the app release. Downloads enforce bounded streaming, HTTPS and the existing GitHub redirect allowlist. Verification precedes installation into the executable path, and sibling staging plus rename avoids publishing partial downloads. Helper management is host-only. Installed helpers are not rehashed on every launch, and no staleness signal is inferred from build hashes. A known download marker names its release; an unmarked helper is labeled locally installed. Redownload controls appear only when a published pin exists. Five v0.1.41 helper assets were fully downloaded and verified before selecting their pins. Download never enables mesh; refreshed readiness presents a separate explicit Enable action.

sections.title: Sidecar lifecycle
sections.summary: The mesh helper communicates over stdio and watches parent stdin for EOF. The manager synchronously launches one owned process, terminates only that child, and ignores output from stopped children; it never sweeps processes sharing a filename. Off is immediate while owned exit settles. Each Studio instance owns a separate ephemeral upstream and per-boot secret. A failed primary startup releases that listener, a failed private bind disables mesh without breaking local Studio or LAN, and closing before settings resolve prevents late automatic startup. Windows GUI-subsystem builds and hidden spawn windows avoid console flashes while preserving pipe handles. Current evidence uses isolated lifecycle and real HTTP handler regressions, without new real mesh activation. Concurrent LAN starts coalesce; Off revokes pending startup, a fresh On waits for old cleanup, and another Off cancels that queued request. LAN authentication and cookie policy remain unchanged.

sections.title: What is proven
sections.summary: Unit tests cover Tailscale owner identity, LAN connect codes, throttle and approval limits, trusted-port secret refusal, host-only routes, helper resolution and unavailable states. Download tests cover checksum mismatch, truncation, redirect restrictions and bounded streaming; pin-format and release-workflow tests cover asset selection and platform inventories. The selected Hoplight release assets were fully downloaded and checked against their published checksums. Current real-handler HTTP fixtures prove concurrent private listeners accept only their own per-boot secrets and release only owned resources. Held-start LAN fixtures prove coalescing, Off winning, a later On surviving cleanup, and another Off cancelling that queued intent. Earlier documentation recorded real LAN and phone Tailscale journeys; this pass does not repeat those journeys or claim new real sign-in, physical-device or cross-platform packaged proof.

sections.title: Local-access certificate dependency and failures
sections.summary: Local network access uses installed OpenSSL to create its self-signed HTTPS certificate. Discovery checks PATH first and standard Git for Windows usr/bin and mingw64/bin locations on Windows. It downloads or installs no certificate executable. Missing OpenSSL produces installation guidance and allows retry. Generation and fingerprint failures remain errors, and the card displays failures from enable, disable, approval, denial and removal operations. Connect codes, explicit device approval and host-only management remain required. The isolated TLS regression starts an ephemeral real HTTPS listener, checks its IP SAN and fingerprint, verifies an unapproved request stays gated, and stops the listener. This is source listener evidence; it does not verify installed binaries or physical devices.
